09:01.evidence: 15 failures from one source within a minute; the address is private campus space, so the guessing host is already inside the network (inference, no flow logs to confirm).

09:03.evidence: A larger second wave (21 after 15) from the same source: 36 failures in 3 minutes and nothing stopped them, so there was no effective lockout.

09:04.evidence: First success from the guessing address, one minute after 36 failures: the password was found and the account is now in the attacker's hands. No second factor is visible. Raised from the dataset's High because this is the moment prevention failed.

09:07.evidence: Bulk modification of 320 files from the attacker's own address 3 minutes after the login: the first change to data, before any host-side symptom.

09:08.evidence: CPU rises on the server itself one minute after the first bulk writes, consistent with an encryption routine. Weak alone (research jobs also load the CPU), strong in this sequence.

09:10.evidence: Encryption is confirmed: 1,200 files, 3.75 times the 320 of 09:07; if the counts are cumulative, about 290 files per minute.

09:12.evidence: An attempt to delete the backups two minutes after encryption began: it only makes sense if the attacker wants the victim unable to restore. It also shows the backups were reachable from the compromised server. The outcome is not in the dataset.

09:13.evidence: First outbound connection of the incident, to an address in no allowlist. It is either data leaving or a command channel; no byte count is given, so I treat it as exfiltration for risk purposes (worst case).

09:15.evidence: Bulk reading of the database two minutes after the outbound channel opened: staging data for theft. The alternative reading, lateral movement, is rejected because no new host or identity appears.

09:18.evidence: Antivirus switched off 8 minutes after encryption started: it needs administrator rights, and it protects the attacker's files from clean-up. It also means antivirus raised nothing during 09:07-09:10.

unused_stages.reconnaissance: No event shows scanning. The attacker's host is already inside the network and the dataset has no network-flow logs, so this is a visibility gap, not proof that it did not happen.
unused_stages.lateral movement: The step from 10.20.4.15 to Research-Server-01 is itself lateral movement from an already compromised host, but the dataset shows only the target side, so events are classified by what happened to the server.

threats.why_likelihood: Confirmed: a login succeeded at 09:04 after 36 failures from one source and nothing stopped the guessing (no effective lockout, no second factor).
threats.why_impact: It opened the way for every later stage, but by itself it gives only what the account may do; the damage is scored in the threats below.

residual.why: MFA and lockout make guessing useless; what remains is a phished second factor or a stolen session. Access goes through the bastion with least privilege, so a stolen account reaches less.

threats.why_likelihood: Confirmed: 320 files modified at 09:07 and 1,200 encrypted at 09:10.
threats.why_impact: Research data and the server's services are lost until restored, and the backups were attacked at the same time (09:12).

residual.why: It cannot be excluded (e-mail, USB, another host). Impact is bounded: alert in 1 minute, isolation in 3, restore from a clean snapshot in 27 minutes, at most 4.5 minutes of data lost.

threats.why_likelihood: A deletion attempt was logged at 09:12; the result is unknown, and a backup reachable from the compromised server is likely to be deletable, so one step below certain.
threats.why_impact: If it succeeds, every other incident becomes unrecoverable and neither RPO nor RTO can be met.

residual.why: Immutable storage, pull-based backups and separate credentials leave only a failure of the storage itself or two colluding approvers. The offline copy keeps the impact at 4: an older state survives, but it loses more than the RPO.

threats.why_likelihood: Two indirect signs, an outbound connection to an unknown IP (09:13) and a database access spike (09:15); no byte volume, so likely but not proven.
threats.why_impact: Research data and possibly personal data of participants leave the university's control, and a backup cannot restore confidentiality; the volume is unknown, so not 5.

residual.why: Egress allowlist and query limits reduce it, but an encrypted channel to an allowed host or a theft by an authorised user remains. Impact stays 4 because recovery controls do not restore confidentiality; this is the largest residual risk.

threats.why_likelihood: Disabling antivirus (09:18) and touching backups need administrator rights, but the log shows no explicit escalation: either the account was already over-privileged or it escalated unseen.
threats.why_impact: Administrator rights let the attacker switch off defences and reach the backups; the effect is large but is counted again in the ransomware and backup threats, so not 5.

residual.why: No standing administrator rights (just-in-time through the bastion), tamper protection on the agents, separate roles for antivirus and backup administration.

controls.preventive: MFA (FIDO2 key or TOTP) for every login through the identity provider; lockout after 5 failures; SSH/RDP of Research-Server-01 reachable only from the bastion.
controls.detective: SIEM rules: 5 or more failures per minute from one source; a success after 10 or more failures from the same source; alert to the SOC on duty.
controls.recovery: Revoke the account's sessions, force a password reset and new MFA enrolment; if the host was touched, restore it from a clean snapshot.

controls.preventive: EDR with application allowlisting and tamper protection; user VLANs have no direct path to the research segment; research files are written by service accounts with minimal rights.
controls.detective: Canary files and file-integrity monitoring (alert on the first changed canary); write-rate and entropy rule; AI anomaly score on file modifications.
controls.recovery: Isolate the host, restore the last clean snapshot from the immutable repository into the recovery environment, verify it, then fail over.

controls.preventive: Immutable repository (object lock, 14-day retention); backups are pulled by the backup server, so the research server holds no delete rights; shortening retention needs two approvers.
controls.detective: Alert on any delete or retention-change call, and on a missing snapshot (nothing new within 2 intervals).
controls.recovery: Restore from the offline second-site copy if the immutable tier is damaged.

controls.preventive: Default-deny outbound firewall with an allowlist; DNS filtering; the database is reached through a service account with a query-rate limit; data at rest encrypted with keys held outside the server.
controls.detective: NetFlow and NIDS alerts on new destinations and on volume; query-rate alert on the database; AI anomaly score on outbound traffic.
controls.recovery: Block the destination, rotate keys and credentials, scope from the logs what left, and report to the university security office and, where required, KZ-CERT.

controls.preventive: Least privilege and no shared administrator accounts; administrator rights granted just-in-time through the bastion with MFA; separate roles for antivirus and backup administration.
controls.detective: Alerts on administrator group changes, new administrator sessions, and any stop or disabling of the EDR agent.
controls.recovery: Rebuild the host from the golden image and rotate all privileged credentials.

coverage.preventive: Source throttled at the firewall by the SOAR playbook
MFA: the password alone gives no session

coverage.detective: AI score on CPU and process activity

coverage.preventive: EDR tamper protection needs a token

steps.component: SIEM correlation + canary/file-integrity alert + AI scorer; SOC on duty confirms
SOAR playbook: firewall quarantine VLAN, identity provider revokes sessions, egress blocked
EDR memory capture + hypervisor disk snapshot to a write-once evidence store; SOC analyst
Backup orchestrator picks the newest clean snapshot in the immutable repository and brings up Research-Server-02 in the recovery environment
Backup orchestrator restores the hot dataset and the database into the recovery environment; cold data follows after production
Integrity verifier: signed hash manifest, malware scan of changed files, database consistency check, canary files; security lead signs off
Failover controller moves the load balancer and DNS to Research-Server-02; identity provider re-enables access with MFA; SOC watches closely

recommendation.mechanism: An offline (air-gapped) copy of the research data at a second site inside Kazakhstan, refreshed daily and restore-tested every quarter.
why: The immutable repository is still online: a compromised backup administrator, a flaw in the storage software or a fire in the server room defeats it. An offline copy at another site is the only layer that none of these reach.

Research datasets with participant data should stay on servers in Kazakhstan (to be confirmed with the university's legal and IT security office), so a foreign cloud is not a free fallback; a partner university or the national research network is.
It is cheap for a university: a weekly or daily rotation of a disk or tape set, no new software, and the restore drill is the proof that it works.
